newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Libya finds no Gulf support for Arab summit call.
newsitem.headline: Libya finds no Gulf support for Arab summit call.

text.p: Some Gulf Arab states have turned down a Libyan call for an Arab summit in Tripoli, Gulf official sources said on Tuesday.
Libyan envoy Mustafa Kharrubi started a Gulf tour last week to rally support for the summit but received mostly unenthusiastic responses, the officials said.
Kharrubi "will find no support for the Libyan call, let alone fly to Libya for a summit," said a Gulf diplomatic source.
The United Nations placed an air and arms embargo against Libya in 1992 over the alleged involvement of two Libyan agents in the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland.

A Gulf official said Gaddafi summit invitations "outlined the need for Arab leaders to meet to lay down a new plan and new strategy for the Arab nation to help it compete politically and economically with the rest of the world."
Kharrubi was quoted in Kuwait as saying that prospects for holding a summit to mark next month's birthday of the Moslem Prophet Mohammad were "good".
Gulf sources said Libya had proposed holding the summit in Cairo -- the Arab League's headquarters -- or in the Moslem holy city of Mecca, Saudi Arabia, if Tripoli was unacceptable.

Arab leaders last met in Egypt in June 1996 to discuss the Middle East peace process after Benjamin Netanyahu was elected Israeli prime minister. In late April Egypt said it was opposed to convening an Arab summit for fear it could complicate the stalled peace talks.
